newsitem.title: UK: Eurobourses down moderately as Wall St slips.
newsitem.headline: Eurobourses down moderately as Wall St slips.

text.p: European stock markets made a jumpy start to a potentially volatile week on Monday but managed to recoup at least part of their sharp opening losses despite a further decline on Wall Street.
The Dow's 148 point slump on Friday gripped European investors from the start but a combination of a strong dollar and steady bond markets restored a measure of calm by the European close.
The dollar ended near its highs against the yen and mark after spending the day trapped in a narrow range with traders also keeping their eyes fixed on U.S. asset markets.
"There's still an awful lot of nervousness about where Wall Street is going," one London equities dealer said.
"It's too early to say whether (the U.S. stock market) has entered a bear market," added NatWest Markets equity strategist David McBain.

Analysts said stock and bond markets faced a stern test this week. U.S. markets are likely to be volatile with key inflation figures coming out along with a series of earnings figures from major technology companies.
The first of those earnings figures were due to be released by microchip leader Intel after American markets closed.
European bond markets steadied after an early dip, with British gilts perking up following figures showing UK producer prices fell 0.1 percent in March.

The U.S. government is due to report March retail inflation data on Tuesday. Although recent economic data has shown robust growth and subdued inflation, a stronger than expected inflation figure would raise fears of another rise in interest rates.
Many market watchers already expect the Federal Reserve's policy-making open market committee to raise rates when it meets next month.

First-quarter earnings reports due from a number of other major U.S. companies, such as Microsoft and General Motors , might also weigh on investors contemplating the prospect that the Dow could fall another five percent.
Traders said investors remained very nervous about where Wall Street was going after losing 10 percent in value since hitting record levels earlier this year.
Major bourses in London, Paris and Frankfurt all ended with moderate losses after sliding heavily at the start. The Dow was about 20 points down as London closed.
Among second tier bourses, the Stockholm, Amsterdam and Madrid markets ended with losses of more than one percent, while Madrid managed a modest gain.
Of the major bourses, Frankfurt fared the worst.
The 30-share blue chip DAX index closed the floor session down nearly two percent at 3,279.90 points, although the strong dollar allowed the market to pare its losses in the post-bourse session.
The IBIS DAX index, which tracks electronic trade, ended the day down 21.72 points at 3,297.52 points, just off a key technical support level at 3,300.
"Maybe the DAX will yet be able to decouple from the U.S.," said one Frankfurt trader of the market's relative resilience.
Very few stocks managed to buck the downward trend, although the dollar-sensitive car sector generally outperformed the market.
A firmer bond market and benign set of British producer price inflation numbers earlier provided some support for the London market, but traders and strategists said they remained cautious.
The benchmark FTSE 100 shed 19.0 points to settle at 4,251.7, as decliners beat advancers by a margin of two to one.
Shares in Royal Bank of Scotland Plc were among the biggest decliners in the FTSE 100, amid continued negative sentiment towards the stock. The shares finished 8-1/2p lower at 521-1/2.
French stocks finished slightly lower, the CAC-40 index closing down 8.43 points, or 0.33 percent, at 2,566.13 after drawing some support from the dollar too.
"At these levels, the dollar's positive for the bourse," one broker said.
The dollar ended European trade holding steady above 1.72 marks and 126.40 yen with dealers keeping a close eye on the Dow.

Sentiment was still bullish, but traders said the market was loath to drive the dollar up for now for several reasons -- its almost straight-line rally last week, nervousness about U.S. asset markets, and the series of U.S. economic data due this week.

Traders said the market was steering clear of pushing dollar/yen up in the face of Japanese authorities' warnings about "excessive" currency moves, though they believed solo intervention by Japan would not damage the dollar much.
"Everyone still wants to buy dollars, but at the same time they're a bit cautious about all this talk about possible intervention," a trader at a Japanese bank said.
CURRENCIES AT 1600 GMT
The dollar was quoted at 1.7240 marks and 126.46 yen compared with 1.7255 marks and 126.15 yen in late European trading on Friday.
STOCK MARKETS --CLOSING INDICES
LONDON - The FTSE-100 index was down 19 points, or 0.44 percent, at 4,251.7
PARIS - The CAC-40 was 8.43 points, or 0.33 percent, at 2,566.13.
FRANKFURT - The 30-share DAX index closed down 60.15 points, or 1.8 percent, at 3,279.47. In later screen trade the IBIS DAX ended down 21.72 points, or 0.65 percent, at 3,297.52.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold ended at $346.55 against $347.20 on Friday. Silver was off six cents at $4.73.
